To define $ \Delta S_{conf} $ we begin by comparing the adsorption of alkanes in five different zeolite structures: MFI, CHA, TON, FAU, and MOR. Depicted in Figure 2A is the relationship between the entropy of an adsorbed molecule (alkanes and permanent gases) and its gas-phase entropy, where the molecular entropy on the surface never exceeds that in the gas phase. While a significant loss in entropy occurs in all five zeolites, the absolute loss in entropy is distinct for each framework. Adsorbates in TON exhibit the largest loss in entropy upon adsorption, while FAU results in the smallest entropic losses. If the molecules were to behave as immobile adsorbates on the surface, the entropy lost upon adsorption ( $ \Delta S_{ads} $) can be approximated to be equal to three degrees of translational freedom, $ ^{3,35,36} $ which can be calculated from statistical mechanics using the Sackur–Tetrode equation $ ^{37} $

$$ S_{\mathrm{trans}}^{0}(T)=S_{\mathrm{Ar},298\mathrm{K}}^{0}+R\ln\left[\left(\frac{m}{m_{\mathrm{Ar}}}\right)^{3/2}\left(\frac{T}{298}\right)^{5/2}\right] $$

ABSTRACT: Confinement of hydrocarbons in nanoscale pockets and pores provides tunable capability for controlling molecules in catalysts, sorbents, and membranes for reaction and separation applications. While computation of the enthalpic interactions of hydrocarbons in confined spaces has improved, understanding and predicting the entropy of confined molecules remains a challenge. Here we show, using a set of nine aluminosilicate zeolite frameworks with broad variation in pore and cavity structure, that the entropy of adsorption can be predicted as a linear combination of rotational and translational entropy. The extent of entropy lost upon adsorption is predicted using only a single material descriptor, the occupiable volume ( $ V_{occ} $). Predictive capability of confined molecular entropy permits an understanding of the relation with adsorption enthalpy, the ability to computationally screen microporous materials, and an understanding of the role of confinement on the kinetics of molecules in confined spaces.

On the basis of this shape-selective feature , highly effective molecular separations and selective catalytic conversions can be achieved within zeolitic structures that are difficult to accomplish with other materials and/or techniques . $ ^ { 1-3 } $ So far, several shape-selectivity mechanisms have been elucidated and applications identified. $ ^{2-18} $ In common molecular sieving, bulky molecules adsorb preferentially over bulkier species as a result of steric constraints imposed by the zeolites' framework, e.g., linear alkane molecules compared to branched isomers. $ ^{19-23} $ Besides this common adsorption competition based on molecular bulkiness, the reverse phenomenon can also occur, i.e., competitive adsorption in favor of the bulkier species. Experiments revealed preferential adsorption of branched alkanes over their linear isomers on specific zeolites with tubular pore systems such as SAPO-5 and Mordenite. $ ^{24-28} $ Molecular simulations indicated that in such zeolites, depending on conditions, branched alkanes are preferentially adsorbed at the expense of linear isomers. $ ^{29-34} $ The present manuscript discusses the mechanisms of shape selectivity in n- and isoalkane adsorption on zeolite MCM-22. This zeolite with IZA code MWW is a relatively new synthetic material that has an unusual and quite complex pore structure. $ ^{35} $ Its framework is composed of two independent pore systems. The enthalpy and the entropy contributions to the Gibbs free energies were calculated at T = 298 K and partial pressure of 1 atm (101325 Pa). The enthalpy (H) of gas-phase pyridine and acetonitrile molecules is defined as the sum of total electronic energy ( $ E_{el} $), internal vibrational energy ( $ E_{v} $), zero-point vibrational energy (ZPVE), as well as the rotational and translational contributions to the internal energy: $ H = E_{el} + E_{v} + ZPVE + E_{R} + E_{t} $. The corresponding calculated entropies (S) includes translational, ( $ S_{t} $) vibrational, ( $ S_{v} $) and rotational ( $ S_{r} $) degrees of freedom: $ S = S_{t} + S_{v} + S_{r} $. All the considered systems are in singlet state, thus the electronic contribution to the entropy is zero. Since both adsorbed molecules are constrained in the zeolite cavity their entropy contributions in the adsorption complexes were corrected as follows: the translational and rotational degrees of freedom were reduced by 1 and 1.28 [37]. The Gibbs free energies of the zeolite support consist of only vibrational and electronic contributions. The expressions of all enthalpy and entropy contributions can be found in Ref. [38].

The first attempts to describe guest-induced flexibility in zeolites were done using molecular dynamics simulations. $ ^{79-82} $ Rigid zeolitic force fields were dynamically modified using transition state theory to include lattice flexibility, and the results obtained by these models were in good agreement with experimental data. $ ^{79-81,83,84} $ It was shown that framework flexibility in silicalite-1 (MFI-type framework) is responsible for the adsorption of large molecules such as isobutane and heptane with inflection behavior at high loadings, $ ^{80} $ while enhanced self-diffusivity at low loadings of short alkanes (i.e. methane and n-butane) was observed. $ ^{81} $ Framework flexibility is also crucial for aromatics adsorption on MFI zeolite, especially at high pressures. $ ^{84,85} $ While the use of rigid zeolitic models led to the underestimation of the aromatics adsorption in MFI zeolite by a factor of two, $ ^{84,85} $ the use of flexible models to simulate diffusion coefficients of various alkanes in silicalite-1 zeolite resulted in a convergence of experimental and theoretical values. $ ^{86} $ Recently by using in situ integrated differential phase contrast scanning transmission electron microscopy (iDPC-STEM) while adsorbing benzene molecules on MFI zeolite, Xiong et al. showed that the MFI structure goes through severe deformations giving another proof of guest-induced flexibility in zeolites (see Fig. 4). $ ^{87} $

2.4.4. Trapdoor. Traditional diﬀusion models primarily consider two types of interactions: those between guest molecules (guest–guest) and those between guest molecules and the zeolite framework (guest–host). However, when cations are present in the zeolite structure, a third interaction—involving guest molecules, the framework, and cations (guest–host-cation)—must also be accounted for. A striking example of such ternary interactions is the well-known ‘‘molecular trapdoor’’. This phenomenon, also referred to as the ‘‘gating effect’’, describes a unique molecular sieving mechanism in certain zeolites and related porous materi- als. Here, extra-framework cations function as dynamic gate- keepers at pore apertures, selectively controlling molecular diffusion to achieve highly discriminative adsorption and separation.9,147,187 To date, ‘‘trapdoor’’ has been observed in several zeolites, including RHO (DNL-6),188–190 CHA (SAPO-34, SSZ-13),147,191,192 MWF (ZSM-25),149,193 HEU (Clinoptilolite),194

The turnover rates of olefin formation during cyclohexanol (CyOH) dehydration within the autoclave reactor initially increase with the local ionic strength within a micropore, and further decrease along ionic strength promotion, shown as a volcano-shaped dependence of TOFs on the ionic strength of zeolites. The local ionic environments with moderate-to-high ionic strength alter the adsorption of uncharged reactants, and stabilize surface intermediates and positively charge the transition states, which eventually increase the reaction rates. But the formation and size of the H₃O⁺(H₂O)ₙ₋₁ in the zeolite pores limit the adsorption of CyOH, e.g., size exclusion effects, and decrease reaction rates. On the other hand, the higher ionic strength results in increased excess chemical potentials of the charged transition states, which in turn raises the activation Gibbs free energies²¹⁻²⁵. In the following appendix , we derive the entropy of adsorption in the case of infinite dilution and show how it may be related to familiar thermodynamic quantities ( cf . eq 5 ) . To begin , we define our adsorption entropy in the limit of infinite dilution via

$$ \Delta s_{\mathrm{ads}}^{\infty}=\lim_{N/V\rightarrow0}\left[\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial N}\right)_{V,T,\mathrm{ads}}-\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial N}\right)_{V,T,\mathrm{gas}}\right] $$

$$ =S_{ads}(N=1,V,T)-S_{gas}(N=1,V,T) $$

where the subscripts “ads” and “gas” labels identify the adsorbed (confined) and gas (bulk) phases, respectively. Given the constraints of a fixed number of molecules (N), volume (V), and temperature (T), it is natural to continue working in the canonical ensemble. (As in the main text, lowercase symbols identify intensive molecular or molar properties, whereas the uppercase indicates an extensive property.) For the molecules that we examine in this work (e.g., rigid molecules with no internal degrees of freedom), the canonical partition function Q may be expressed as

$$ \begin{aligned}Q(N,V,T)&=Q_{trans}(N,V,T)Q_{rot}(N,V,T)\\&\quad\times Z(N,V,T)\end{aligned} $$

where $ Q_{trans} $ and $ Q_{rot} $ are the translational and rotational partition functions (which are unaffected by confinement) and Z is the configurational partition function. The translational and rotational partition functions are available in the usual statistical mechanics texts $ ^{44,45} $ but are ultimately unimportant for the derivation that follows.

descriptor_candidates.name: confinement_volume_ratio_descriptor
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: The entropy loss upon adsorption (ΔS/R) increases monotonically with the ratio of molecular volume to occupiable pore volume, and a descriptor combining molecular volume with accessible void volume and pore-length ratio will reduce MAE of ΔS/R below a 14-input neural-network baseline. Falsified if removing Vol/AV dependence (permutation) does not degrade MAE, or if the monotonic trend breaks across FAU-like (large cavity) vs TON-like (channel) frameworks.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Evidence E02 reports adsorption entropy predicted from occupiable volume alone (known mechanism); E01 shows framework-dependent entropy loss (TON largest, FAU smallest). Confinement restricts translational degrees of freedom proportionally to the fraction of pore space the molecule occupies; the local pore length ratio (lsd_p/lsd_f) distinguishes channel-like from cage-like confinement, where cage rotation retains more freedom.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Permutation importance of Vol and AV terms ~0 in MAE reduction, or sign-inverted correlation between descriptor and measured ΔS/R on held-out zeolite/adsorbate pairs.

descriptor_candidates.name: shape_asymmetry_confinement_descriptor
descriptor_candidates.formula: log( (SPAN * GeDi) / (Vol ** (1.0/3.0)) ) * (1.0 - AV / (AV + lsd_f * lsd_p * lsd_p))
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Molecular shape anisotropy (SPAN/GeDi relative to cube-root volume) modulates entropy loss beyond what total volume captures: elongated or planar molecules lose more rotational entropy in channels but less in cages. A descriptor coupling shape anisotropy to cage/channel geometry (via AV and lsd products) will lower MAE of ΔS/R; falsified if adding this descriptor to a model already using Vol, AV, and size moments does not significantly reduce MAE (e.g., paired test at α = 0.05).
descriptor_candidates.rationale: E04 documents shape-selective confinement effects where linear vs branched molecules have distinct adsorption states; E07 shows molecular symmetry alters confined dynamics. Rotation of anisotropic molecules is frozen differently in channels (lsd_f-limited) vs cages, so a shape×geometry cross term is a mechanistically motivated new combination, not a restatement of the volume-only relation.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: The cross-term descriptor yields no statistically significant MAE improvement over baseline + volume-only descriptor, or its coefficient has the opposite sign to the channel-freezing prediction across framework classes.

descriptor_candidates.name: inertia_gated_mobility_descriptor
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Rotational entropy loss is governed by the geometric mean of principal moments of inertia relative to accessible surface area, gated by how the molecule's smallest dimension (PBF, approximate breadth) compares to the largest free sphere diameter: when PBF approaches lsd_f, rotation is fully arrested and ΔS/R saturates near the translational-loss value from the Sackur–Tetrode-like limit (E01, E05). Falsified if the PMI-derived term's contribution to MAE is not reduced when restricted to the high-confinement regime (PBF/lsd_f → 1), where the hypothesis predicts descriptor irrelevance.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: E05 shows adsorbed entropy corrections reduce translational and rotational degrees of freedom by fixed factors; E09 derives adsorption entropy from translational/rotational partition functions. PMI triple captures the rotational partition function's dependence on the inertia tensor; LabuteASA scales the accessible configurational space; PBF vs lsd_f measures steric gating of rotation (E10: molecules can compress but rotation through windows is harder).
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: In the subset with PBF/lsd_f > 0.9, replacing PMI terms by a constant leaves MAE unchanged (rotation already frozen, descriptor should be inert); if PMI terms still improve MAE there, the gating mechanism is falsified. Also falsified if the inertia term never contributes outside noise level in the low-confinement regime.

descriptor_candidates.name: aperture_to_breadth_gating_descriptor
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss is largest when the molecule's smallest dimension (PBF) approaches or exceeds the pore aperture (lsd_p): near gate-fitting molecules lose rotational degrees of freedom abruptly, while in oversized pores the loss scales mainly with fractional volume occupancy. A multiplicative gating of the aperture/breadth mismatch by the volume fraction will reduce MAE of ΔS/R below the 14-input baseline. Falsified if the PBF/lsd_p term's permutation importance is ~0, or if the descriptor-to-ΔS/R correlation in the PBF/lsd_p > 0.8 subset has the opposite sign to the predicted positive slope.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference from E10: molecules can compress to enter pores down to ~80% of their free size, and rotation through windows is harder than translation, so aperture-to-breadth proximity should mark the onset of rotational freezing. E01 shows framework-dependent entropy loss (TON vs FAU), consistent with an aperture-controlled regime. Source evidence: E10, E01; the gating multiplication by volume fraction is our inference.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Permutation of PBF or lsd_p in the descriptor leaves MAE unchanged; or ΔS/R vs descriptor slope is not positive in the high-gating (PBF/lsd_p near or above 1) regime; or descriptor performance is not better than the retained volume-ratio descriptor alone (paired MAE comparison).

descriptor_candidates.name: inertial_surface_translational_loss_descriptor
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Beyond mass (MW), the full inertia tensor (via the geometric mean of PMIs) governs how much rotational entropy survives confinement relative to gas phase; molecules with high inertia-per-unit-mass (large, extended rotors) lose proportionally more entropy in confined pores whose local aperture (lsd_p) is small relative to their accessible surface (LabuteASA). A descriptor combining inertia-per-mass with a surface-to-aperture confinement factor will lower MAE of ΔS/R. Falsified if the PMI-derived term adds no MAE improvement beyond MW alone, or if the residual after fitting shows no monotonic trend with the inertia term.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence: E09 derives adsorption entropy from translational and rotational partition functions, which depend on the inertia tensor, not just mass; E05 shows rotational entropy reduction factors upon adsorption. Inference: expressing inertia per unit mass isolates shape-dependent rotational freezing from trivial mass scaling, and the ASA/lsd_p^2 factor captures how much pore wall the molecule can touch relative to aperture size.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Replacing the PMI product by MW alone (same formula structure) yields statistically indistinguishable MAE (paired test α=0.05); or the descriptor's coefficient sign contradicts the prediction (more inertia-per-mass → more entropy loss) on held-out data.

descriptor_candidates.name: channel_cage_dimensional_confinement_descriptor
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss depends on the interplay between molecular extension (SPAN, GeDi) and pore dimensionality: channel-like pores (small lsd_f × lsd_p product relative to molecular extension) freeze more degrees of freedom than cage-like pores, and framework packing density per accessible volume modulates the configurational space available. A descriptor combining molecular extension with the pore dimensional product and framework packing (density/AV) will reduce MAE of ΔS/R. Falsified if MAE of this descriptor is worse than the retained volume-only descriptor, or if framework class (FAU-like vs TON-like) residuals show no systematic sign difference consistent with the channel-freezing prediction.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence: E01 reports TON (channel) loses most entropy, FAU (cage) least; E04 shows shape-matched adsorption states differ even for chemically similar molecules. Inference: the ratio of molecular long axes (SPAN·GeDi) to the lsd_f·lsd_p area-like pore term distinguishes channel vs cage confinement without reusing Vol/AV as the primary ratio, adding shape-extension information the retained descriptor lacks.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: No significant MAE improvement over the retained confinement_volume_ratio_descriptor (paired test α=0.05); or residuals do not differ systematically between channel-dominated (TON, MFI, MOR) and cage-dominated (FAU, CHA) frameworks; or nonfinite values exceed 5% of rows.

descriptor_candidates.name: surface_to_framework_contact_descriptor
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss upon adsorption increases with the fraction of molecular surface that can make contact with pore walls relative to the framework's gravimetric surface area: molecules whose LabuteASA is large compared with the framework ASA per unit pore scale, and whose volume is large relative to the lsd_f x lsd_p x lsd_p local pore dimension product, retain fewer translational/rotational configurations. Adding this descriptor to the 14-input neural network will reduce the MAE of entropy loss/R below the current retained baseline (MAE_R = 0.5554). Falsified if the descriptor's permutation importance is ~0, or if residuals show no monotonic trend with the LabuteASA/ASA term within framework classes.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Mechanism (source: E01, E02): adsorbed entropy never exceeds gas-phase entropy and loss is framework-dependent, with confinement removing translational/rotational degrees of freedom. Inference: contact-area-based configurational restriction should scale with the ratio of molecular accessible surface to a framework surface-scale term; this uses surface geometry (LabuteASA, ASA) rather than the already-retained Vol/AV volume ratio, giving a mechanistically distinct axis. The +1.0 offsets and the lsd product guarantee finiteness (fixing the nonfinite failure of round 1's inertia descriptor).
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Permuting LabuteASA or ASA within the descriptor leaves MAE unchanged (paired test alpha = 0.05); or the descriptor-to-deltaS/R slope is not positive on held-out zeolite/adsorbate pairs; or MAE_R does not improve on 0.5554.

descriptor_candidates.name: rotor_anisotropy_aperture_descriptor
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Molecules with high moment-of-inertia anisotropy (PMI1/PMI3, e.g., elongated rotors) lose rotational entropy selectively in pores whose aperture (lsd_p) is small relative to the molecule's minimum dimension (PBF), because only the slowest tumbling mode is frozen when the molecule barely fits the window. The product of the log anisotropy ratio and the PBF/lsd_p gating factor will reduce MAE of entropy loss/R below the retained baseline. Falsified if the anisotropy term's contribution vanishes after replacing PMI1/PMI3 by a constant, or if the descriptor-deltaS/R correlation has the opposite sign in the PBF/lsd_p > 0.8 subset.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence: E09 derives adsorption entropy from rotational partition functions that depend on the full inertia tensor; E07 shows molecular symmetry alters confined dynamics; E05 shows rotational degrees of freedom are reduced (factor ~1.28) upon adsorption. Inference: only inertia anisotropy (not inertia magnitude, which round 2 showed adds nothing beyond MW) carries independent information, and it should matter only near aperture-fitting conditions (E10: molecules penetrate pores down to ~80% of free size, rotation through windows is hardest). The +1.0 offsets ensure all values are finite and positive.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Substituting a constant for the PMI ratio yields statistically indistinguishable MAE (paired test alpha = 0.05); or residual sign in the high-gating regime contradicts the predicted positive slope; or the descriptor underperforms the retained aperture_to_breadth_gating_descriptor.

descriptor_candidates.name: extension_packing_window_descriptor
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss peaks when a molecule's long-axis extension (SPAN) and middle-axis spread (GeDi) simultaneously exceed the local pore window scales (lsd_f, lsd_p), forcing simultaneous loss of one translational and multiple rotational modes; framework packing (density relative to accessible pore volume AV) modulates the residual configurational space. This extension-versus-window cross descriptor, combined with a compactness-style packing term, will reduce MAE of entropy loss/R below the retained baseline. Falsified if MAE_R is not better than 0.5554, or if residuals across channel-like (TON/MFI/MOR) vs cage-like (FAU/CHA) frameworks show no sign pattern consistent with stronger freezing when SPAN/lsd_f and GeDi/lsd_p are jointly large.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence: E01 shows TON (channel) produces the largest entropy loss and FAU (cage) the smallest, implying pore dimensionality/dimensionality-matching matters; E04 shows close shape matching creates distinct adsorption states for similar molecules. Inference: the product of two extension-to-window ratios captures simultaneous two-axis squeezing, which a single aperture ratio (already retained) cannot; the density/AV packing term acts as a framework-compactness modulator on the source numerical scale (no unverified units assigned). All terms are strictly positive under the offsets, avoiding the nonfinite failure mode of round 1.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Paired MAE comparison (alpha = 0.05) shows no improvement over the retained baseline; or permuting SPAN or GeDi within the descriptor does not change MAE; or the framework-class residual pattern (channel vs cage) contradicts the predicted stronger entropy loss at high SPAN/lsd_f x GeDi/lsd_p; or more than 5% nonfinite values.

retained.name: confinement_volume_ratio_descriptor
retained.hypothesis: The entropy loss upon adsorption (ΔS/R) increases monotonically with the ratio of molecular volume to occupiable pore volume, and a descriptor combining molecular volume with accessible void volume and pore-length ratio will reduce MAE of ΔS/R below a 14-input neural-network baseline. Falsified if removing Vol/AV dependence (permutation) does not degrade MAE, or if the monotonic trend breaks across FAU-like (large cavity) vs TON-like (channel) frameworks.

retained.name: aperture_to_breadth_gating_descriptor
retained.hypothesis: Entropy loss is largest when the molecule's smallest dimension (PBF) approaches or exceeds the pore aperture (lsd_p): near gate-fitting molecules lose rotational degrees of freedom abruptly, while in oversized pores the loss scales mainly with fractional volume occupancy. A multiplicative gating of the aperture/breadth mismatch by the volume fraction will reduce MAE of ΔS/R below the 14-input baseline. Falsified if the PBF/lsd_p term's permutation importance is ~0, or if the descriptor-to-ΔS/R correlation in the PBF/lsd_p > 0.8 subset has the opposite sign to the predicted positive slope.
